h: פּוּרִים, מַאֲמָר ג׳ Purim — Maamar Gimmel

p: He said to him, "Their years are great,
for they eat and drink and say,
עוֹנֶג שַׁבָּת עוֹנֶג יוֹם טוֹב וְכוּ׳
HaKadosh Baruch Hu said to him,
an evil eye upon their festivals;
behold, I will make you fall before them,
and they will add for themselves one festival
these are the days of Purim," etc.
looked upon this with an evil eye,
and did not believe that any holiness is found
For this sprouts from the root of the serpent,
And there is a hint to this in the Gemara
"Where is Haman alluded to in the Torah?
That is, there it is written,
to eat from, have you eaten?"
For this is the root of the kelipah of Haman:
to be immersed in the lust for eating
for the sake of bodily pleasure,
like the seduction of the serpent.
the eye of Bilam the wicked was blinded.
He said: He Who is pure and holy,
and His servants are pure and holy,
should He gaze upon such a thing?" etc.
as is known that this desire
also derives from the blemish of the serpent,
that they would make yet another, new festival
And this is as they said (Megillah 7b):
"A person is obligated to become intoxicated
the inner holiness of Yisrael becomes clarified:
that even the matter of the pleasure
in the manner of what they said (Sanhedrin 38a):
so that they will say something," etc.,
"Through three things a person is recognized:
when awareness is taken from him,
then the distinction becomes recognized and clarified
between the holiness of Yisrael and the nations:
that in Yisrael, even in matters
of the pleasures of this world,
they begin with words of Torah
That is, in Yisrael there becomes clarified,
the inner core of their intent,
that is found in eating and drinking;
they begin with words of Torah,

paragraphs.text: Esther Rabbah 7:12 — “Haman said: Their teeth are large: they eat and drink and say, 'Shabbos delight, festival delight,' reducing the world's wealth. One day in seven is Shabbos; one in thirty is Rosh Chodesh; in Nisan, Pesach; in Sivan, Shavuos; in Tishrei, Rosh Hashanah, the great fast, and Sukkos. ... The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Wicked one, you cast an evil eye upon their festivals! I shall cast you down before them, and they shall add another festival over your downfall—the days of Purim.” The Midrash's response makes Haman's attack upon holy festivity the very occasion for an additional holy festival. Rav Tzadok explains why eating and drinking, the objects of Haman's accusation, become the form of its celebration.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 15 — “His accusation was that the eating of Shabbos and Pesach clarifies the whole year’s eating in holiness … At the Omer it was clarified that even those who resemble an animal also have holiness.” Rav Tzadok there places Haman’s denial in the Omer season and shows how it was answered: the barley offering, animal fodder, proves that bodily eating too can carry holiness.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 31a — “Because of this, the eye of Bilaam the wicked was blinded. He said: Can One Who is pure and holy, and Whose servants are pure and holy, look upon such a matter? His eye was immediately blinded, as it is written: 'The utterance of the man whose eye is closed.'” The preceding statement interprets 'Who has counted the dust of Yaakov and numbered Israel's couplings?' as God awaiting the drop from which a righteous person will be formed. Bilaam refuses to recognize Divine concern and holiness within marital bodily life; this is the precise analogy Rav Tzadok draws to Haman's attitude toward eating.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 38a — “He said to them: My sons, are you putting thorns into my eyes? Rabbi Chiya said to him: Rabbi, do not be distressed. Yayin, wine, has the numerical value seventy, and sod, secret, has the numerical value seventy. Wine entered; the secret emerged.” Rabbi had urged that Rabbi Chiya's sons be given more wine so that they would speak. Their ensuing statement about the ending of the patriarchal and exilarchic houses pained him; Rabbi Chiya explained that the wine had brought a hidden teaching into speech. Rav Tzadok applies the principle of disclosed inwardness, rather than the specific political content of their statement.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 65b — “Rabbi Ilai said: A person is recognized through three things: his cup, his purse, and his anger. Some add: also through his laughter.” The saying treats drinking as a disclosure of character. Rav Tzadok joins it to the preceding emergence of a secret, explaining how the Purim feast may reveal the inward direction of the participant.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Resisei Layla 49 — “In a time of drunkenness, when the body acts without the soul's reflection … then comes the clarification that the power of Amalek is not planted in the bodies of Yisrael at all.” Rav Tzadok there gives the mechanism of “a person is recognized through his cup”: once the guiding mind is removed, only what is rooted in the body itself acts, and so Yisrael's bodily nature is shown to be holy.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pekudei 6 — “Achashverosh imagined his heart was merry with wine, but through the wine his vileness was revealed … in Yisrael, the wine revealed the depths of their heart, opening their mouths to songs and praises.” Rav Tzadok there reads the same Megillah 12b as a contrast: wine discloses the inner self of both, and in Yisrael the inner self is Torah and praise.
